catalog_quote: Another research question connected to the above mentioned observation concerns the distribution of “prominence” between the syllables of a word. A common assumption is that in disyllabic words, one syllable is “weak” whereas the other is “strong”, and that this imbalance in prominence conditions or restricts the application of tone sandhi. Wenzhou has typically been regarded as a “right-prominent” language (Chen 2000; Yip 1999). This would entail the expectation that in the tone sandhi patterns, the rightmost syllables should generally be longer and carry more complex tonal contours. As can be seen in the descriptions of the tone sandhi contours above, this generalization does not describe the findings for the young speakers accurately. While it is true that some tone sandhi patterns display an uneven distribution of duration that is independent of the segments of the syllables, these uneven distributions cannot be generalized across the entire data set. Rather, they seem to be connected to certain types of tones. For example, a dipping tone on the first syllable, combined with anything else than a dipping tone on the second syllable, will come out as a short low level tone in the tone sandhi contour. However, the same tone combined with another dipping tone will surface in an tone sandhi contour which is balanced for duration.

new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Copies checked (16 PDFs, all with text layers; extracted text extractions in txt/; present and accurate). (1) Featured quote: Scholz 2012 LOT 305, txt/ lines 1948-1957, printed p. 40 in sec. 2.5.4 'Generalizations on the tone sandhi contours in Wenzhou Chinese' -- the quoted five sentences are there word for word ('Wenzhou has typically been regarded as a "right-prominent" language (Chen 2000; Yip 1999). This would entail the expectation that.. Rather, they seem to be connected to certain types of tones.'); the only difference is a paragraph break between 'complex tonal contours.' and 'As can be seen', which I count as verbatim. The surrounding section continues exactly as the compilers sum…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Wenzhou is an eight-tone Wu variety with right-dominant disyllabic tone sandhi (word-final tone selects the melody; initial-syllable contrasts neutralise). There is no lexical (contrastive) word stress; statements about 'stress' concern relative prominence inside the disyllabic sandhi word and they conflict: (a) the native description (Zhengzhang 1964, as reported by Bao 1990:107 and echoed by Duanmu 1990:147-8, Rose 2004:241) puts stress on the FIRST syllable of a bisyllabic word, shifting to the SECOND when the first syllable carries an entering (ru, 323/212 dipping) tone, with the weak syllable realised as a short 'light' (qingsheng) tone; (b) generative accounts (Chen 2000; Yip 1999) class Wenzhou as right-prominent because the final syllable keeps its tone; (c) instrumental work finds clear first-syllable (trochaic) prominence only in ping+qu (I+III) words and roughly even prominence elsewhere (Rose 2004, 2011), and no data-wide asymmetry in young speakers, prominence differences being tied to particular tone classes (Scholz 2012:40). Net: prominence within the word is tone-conditioned, not positionally fixed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: Entering-tone (ru, dipping 323/212/313) first syllables surface short and low and are described as stressless, with prominence on the second syllable (Zhengzhang per Bao 1990:107,109; Scholz 2012:40 generalization 17b); ping+qu (I+III) words are trochaic with a 'light' atonic second syllable (Rose 2004:240-1; Zhengzhang 1964:108 per Rose); Rose 2011 finds the trochaic pattern in his male but not his female speaker; verb-object phrases take phrasal prosody with the tone kept on the non-head (object) and the verb reduced to low (Chen 2000 per Scholz 2012:44-45).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the disyllabic (lexical) tone-sandhi word / bisyllabic phrase in citation-style elicitation; Scholz's data are carrier-sentence productions by ten 18-20-year-old Lucheng (Wenzhou city) speakers; Rose's are isolated disyllabic words from one or two city speakers recorded in the 1980s; Zhengzhang describes the city variety impressionistically. Phrase-level prominence (non-head stress, focus) is treated separately in Scholz chs. 3-5 and Chen 2000 ch. 11.
new_statements.identity_note: All first-hand statements concern the Wenzhou city variety (Scholz 2012: ten speakers aged 18-20 born and raised in Lucheng district, Wenzhou; Rose 1994-2011: one or two city speakers recorded in the 1980s; Zhengzhang 1964 as reported by Bao 1990 fn.10: 'the variety spoken in the city proper'). Glottolog ouji1238 'Wenzhou' is the Oujiang Wu languoid; Rose 2016 (also saved) describes Wencheng, a different Oujiang locality, and is not used for the statement.

sources.note: Ch. 2 is a phonology sketch (segments, phonotactics, 8 citation tones, disyllabic sandhi). Sec. 2.5.4 p. 40: literature treats Wenzhou as 'right-prominent' (Chen 2000; Yip 1999), but her young speakers show no general durational/tonal asymmetry favouring the final syllable; uneven prominence is tied to particular tone classes (e.g. a dipping/entering tone on syllable 1 surfaces short and low). No claim of lexical stress; prosodic headedness discussed only at phrase level (non-head prominence, after Chen 2000/Duanmu).
